title: Kubernetes Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Kubernetes lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: A cluster and its tools
entries.summary: A cluster is a group of machines managed together. kubectl is a command-line tool that asks the Kubernetes API about that cluster.
notes: Check the target context before any command that changes resources.

entries.name: Check the current context
entries.summary: A context chooses a cluster, user and sometimes namespace. Read it first so you know where a command would act.

example.code:
kubectl config current-context
kubectl config get-contexts

notes: Never assume the current context is a safe practice environment.

entries.name: Pods hold containers
entries.summary: A Pod is Kubernetes' smallest runnable unit. Containers in one Pod share some resources, such as the network address.

example.code:
Pod: club-web
Container: web server
Pod network address: shared by containers in that Pod

notes: Do not expect an individual Pod name or address to last forever.

entries.name: Deployments manage replicas
entries.summary: A Deployment describes how many matching Pods should run and how their template looks. A replica is one copy.

example.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: club-web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: club-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: club-web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:stable

notes: The selector must match the labels on the Pod template.

entries.name: Labels group resources
entries.summary: A label is a key-value marker attached to a resource. Selectors find resources with matching labels.
notes: Labels should not hold secret or sensitive values.

entries.name: Inspect resources
entries.summary: get lists resources. describe gives a detailed human-readable view with events that can explain problems.

example.code:
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe deployment club-web

notes: A resource existing in another namespace does not mean it exists in the current one.

entries.name: Services give a stable route
entries.summary: A Service gives a stable way to reach a selected group of Pods. This example is internal to the cluster.

example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: club-web
spec:
  selector:
    app: club-web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
  type: ClusterIP

notes: A Service with no matching healthy Pods cannot serve the app.

entries.name: ConfigMaps hold ordinary settings
entries.summary: A ConfigMap stores non-secret configuration. An application may read selected values through environment variables or files.

example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: club-settings
data:
  WELCOME_TEXT: "Hello, club"

notes: Use the appropriate secret-management approach for real credentials; a ConfigMap is not one.

entries.name: Resource requests and limits
entries.summary: Requests help schedule a container. Limits bound some resource use. CPU m means one thousandth of a CPU unit.

example.code:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "100m"
    memory: "64Mi"
  limits:
    cpu: "200m"
    memory: "128Mi"

notes: A request is not a measurement of current usage.

entries.name: Readiness and liveness
entries.summary: A readiness check asks whether a container should receive traffic. A liveness check asks whether Kubernetes should restart it.

example.code:
Readiness fails -> stop sending Service traffic to that Pod
Liveness fails repeatedly -> container may restart

notes: Do not use a restart as the answer to every readiness problem.

entries.name: Read logs and rollout state
entries.summary: Logs show the program's messages. Rollout status reports progress while a Deployment changes its Pods.

example.code:
kubectl logs deployment/club-web
kubectl rollout status deployment/club-web

notes: A successful rollout does not prove every user journey works.

entries.name: Namespaces organise a cluster
entries.summary: A namespace groups namespaced resources. It helps separate teams or practice work, but is not by itself a complete security boundary.

example.code:
Namespace: club-practice
Deployment: club-web inside club-practice
Service: club-web inside club-practice

notes: Delete only a namespace you created for disposable practice; it may contain many resources.
